pointers.sentence: The modules of `django/utils/` that serve every part of Django and belong to none, with `django.core.exceptions`: the lazy values, lazy objects and cached properties by which code puts off work until it is needed, the importing of code named by a dotted path, the data structures and the helpers for text, values and paths that the request cycle and the ORM share, the exceptions they raise, and the tools with which Django deprecates its own API and names its versions.
`django/utils/` is where Django keeps its answers, and `django/core/exceptions.py` holds many of the exceptions that its parts share.

`django/utils/functional.py` gives Django three ways to put off work, each with its own object, and they differ in when the work is done and whether its result is kept.
The result is not kept, and the docstring of `lazy` says so: each use calls the function again (`django/utils/functional.py:lazy`).

A `LazyObject` holds the object in `LazyObject._wrapped`, which starts as a marker called `empty`; the first time an attribute is read, set or deleted on it, or one of the special methods it forwards is used, it calls `LazyObject._setup`, which a subclass writes to put the object there, and from then on it passes those straight to that object (`django/utils/functional.py:LazyObject`).

The first read of the attribute on an instance calls the method and writes the result into the instance's own `__dict__`, under the attribute's name; and since the descriptor defines neither `__set__` nor `__delete__`, Python looks in the instance's dictionary before it asks the descriptor, so every later read finds the value there and never reaches the method (`django/utils/functional.py:cached_property.__get__`).

It first tries to import the whole path as a module; then it imports the module up to the path's last dot and returns that module's attribute of the last name, raising `ImportError` if there is none, so that a path naming a module returns the module, and a submodule wins over an attribute of the same name (`django/utils/module_loading.py:import_string`).

`autodiscover_modules` imports a module of a given name from every installed application, as the admin does for each application's admin.py, and passes over an application that has no such module; an error raised inside a module that does exist is raised again (`django/utils/module_loading.py:autodiscover_modules`).

Django also asks a callable what it accepts before it calls it, through `django/utils/inspect.py`: in debug mode `Signal.connect` refuses a receiver that has no parameter for arbitrary keyword arguments (`django/dispatch/dispatcher.py:Signal.connect`), and `Paginator.count` calls an object list's `count` only if it is a method, not a built-in one, that takes no arguments, and otherwise takes the list's length (`django/core/paginator.py:Paginator.count`).

Both modules have their sections: [Importing by name: `import_string` and `autodiscover_modules`](utils/importing.md) and [Asking a callable what it accepts: `django/utils/inspect.py`](utils/inspect.md).
A `MultiValueDict` is a `dict` whose values are lists: indexing it gives the last value under a key, and `MultiValueDict.getlist` gives them all (`django/utils/datastructures.py:MultiValueDict`).

Beside it in `django/utils/datastructures.py` are `CaseInsensitiveMapping`, a mapping whose keys are looked up whatever their case, on which a request's and a response's headers are built; `OrderedSet`, which keeps distinct items in the order in which they were added; and `ImmutableList`, a tuple that answers most of a list's methods for changing it with an `AttributeError` and a message of its maker's choosing ([Data structures: `MultiValueDict` and its neighbours](utils/datastructures.md)).

`Node`, the tree of `django/utils/tree.py`, is what a `Q` and a query's where clause are built from: a list of children, a connector that joins them, and a mark that negates the whole ([`filter`, `exclude` and `Q` objects](querysets/filters.md)) (`django/utils/tree.py:Node`).

`force_str` makes anything a `str`, decoding bytes as UTF-8 unless told otherwise, and `force_bytes` makes anything bytes; `smart_str` and `smart_bytes` do the same but return a lazy value unchanged, so that a lazy translation stays lazy (`django/utils/encoding.py:smart_str`).
The same module turns an internationalized resource identifier into a URI and back, and a file's path into the path of a URL ([Text and bytes: `django/utils/encoding.py`](utils/encoding.md)).

`django/utils/text.py` has the helpers that the template filters and the model and storage code call for text: `Truncator`, `slugify`, `get_valid_filename`, `capfirst` and others ([Text helpers: `Truncator` and `django/utils/text.py`](utils/text.md)).

`django/utils/text.py` has the helpers that the template filters and the model and storage code call for text: `Truncator`, `slugify`, `get_valid_filename`, `capfirst` and others ([Text helpers: `Truncator` and `django/utils/text.py`](utils/text.md)).
Values arrive as text, from a database that stores dates as text, as SQLite does, or from a serialized fixture, and Django reads them with `django/utils/dateparse.py`.

`parse_datetime` tries the standard library's `datetime.datetime.fromisoformat` first, and Django's own pattern only where that fails; for text in neither form it returns `None`, and for text that Django's pattern reads but that names an impossible date it raises `ValueError` (`django/utils/dateparse.py:parse_datetime`).

`safe_join` joins paths and refuses a result outside the first of them, which is how a storage and a template loader keep a name from reaching outside their directory ([Paths and archives: `safe_join`, `safe_makedirs` and `extract`](utils/paths.md)) (`django/utils/_os.py:safe_join`).
`django/core/exceptions.py` defines the exceptions its docstring calls global, many of them raised in one part of Django and caught in another.

`SynchronousOnlyOperation` is raised by a function marked with `async_unsafe`, such as `BaseDatabaseWrapper.connect`, when it is called in a thread where an event loop is running, unless the environment variable `"DJANGO_ALLOW_ASYNC_UNSAFE"` is set (`django/utils/asyncio.py:async_unsafe`).
A later release removes it (`docs/internals/release-process.txt`).
At this commit there are two such classes, `RemovedInDjango2028Warning`, a `DeprecationWarning`, and `RemovedInDjango2029Warning`, a `PendingDeprecationWarning` (`django/utils/deprecation.py`).

Following DEP 20, the releases that were to be Django 7.0 and 7.1 are Django 2028 and 2029, and the warning classes are renamed with them: RemovedInDjango70Warning became `RemovedInDjango2028Warning`, and RemovedInDjango71Warning became `RemovedInDjango2029Warning` (`docs/releases/6.2.txt`).

`warn_about_external_use` warns only when the code that used the feature is outside Django: it walks up the stack to that caller, and stays silent when the caller is Django's own code, so that one deprecated feature built on another does not set off a second warning (`django/utils/deprecation.py:warn_about_external_use`).

`django.VERSION` is a `VersionTuple`, at this commit `(6, 2, 0, "alpha", 0)`, and `django.__version__` the string `get_version` makes from it, here `"6.2.dev20260926051415"`: for an alpha of iteration 0 whose `django` package is in a git repository, `".dev"` and the time, in UTC, of the commit checked out there follow the number (`django/utils/version.py:get_version`).
